title: Object, Network, Field: Three Modes of Cultural Landscape Significance and the Limits of Boundary Instruments
content: Heritage instruments require mapped boundaries, yet many culturally significant landscapes are organized by relationships, movement, or spiritual intensity rather than edges. This article identifies three modes of cultural landscape significance (spatial, relational, and metaphysical), represented by object, network, and field models. Boundaries suit spatial significance but misrepresent the other modes. Ethnographic testimony from Indigenous communities on the Colorado Plateau and in southern Nevada, alongside comparative cases from Iran, highland New Guinea, Türkiye, and the Peruvian Andes, shows that bounding unbounded significance produces empirical errors and an ethical cost termed cultural triage. Ceremonial networks respond differently to loss: Southern Paiute functions may relocate; Hopi routes may change to reach immovable places; Navajo places may be substitutable or fixed; and Rainbow Bridge offerings resumed after floodwaters receded. Application to Bears Ears suggests four refinements: broader metaphysical evidence criteria, multiple network nodes at one place, independently significant links, and time within each mode. The article outlines implications for Section 106 ethnographic documentation and distinguishes representational adequacy from institutional durability, illustrated by the Bears Ears Commission’s 2026 dissolution.
